name: Neck cream / retinoid for necklines

image.caption: Crema redefinición rostro y cuello pieles normales a mixtas - Lift Contour Face & Neck Cream Normal to combination skins

lead: Neck creams are topical products used to improve lines, laxity, crepiness and pigmentation on the neck and decolletage, and some contain retinoids or other actives. They are a low-intensity option among skincare-oriented users who want a smoother, more even neck.

Ingredients such as retinoids, N-acetyl glucosamine and vitamin K2 are proposed to support skin matrix, hydration or cellular energy. Published studies are small and product-specific: an 85-woman study of a neck cream used twice daily for three months assessed texture, fine lines, laxity and hydration, and a 16-week study of a firming cream reported changes in neck and decolletage signs of aging.

paras: People apply the cream to the neck and chest once or twice daily as part of a skincare routine, often alongside sunscreen. Studies run about 12 to 16 weeks, which is the timeframe users commonly expect for visible skin changes.
Irritation is a general concern for topicals, particularly retinoids, and a case of allergic contact dermatitis to an ingredient in a neck cream has been reported.

web.title: Retinoids in the treatment of skin aging
Botulinum A exotoxin for the aging neck

angle.text: Neck creams, some containing retinoids, are applied to improve skin texture and tone so neck lines, laxity and pigmentation look less visible. Small product-specific studies lasting 12 to 16 weeks report improvement in skin signs.

lead: Neck creams are topical products marketed to smooth lines, firm crepey skin and even out colour on the neck and decolletage, and some contain retinoids such as retinol. People use them so that the neck matches a well-cared-for face: smoother, more evenly toned neck skin reads as younger and makes the transition from jawline to neck look cleaner.

The idea behind neck-specific formulas is that neck skin differs from facial skin. One group describing a retinol, tripeptide and glaucine cream said the neck has thinner skin and a more delicate dermal layer [1], and another manufacturer-linked study framed neck care as part of consumer interest in moving anti-ageing from the face to other regions [2]. Retinoids are the family of vitamin A derivatives, from over-the-counter retinol and retinal to prescription tretinoin, whose effects on collagen and skin texture are best documented on the face [3][4][5].

Published neck-specific research consists of small trials of 12 to 16 weeks, several linked to the products' makers, that report improvement in wrinkles, texture, tone and hydration [6][2][7][1]. Surgical and injectable options such as platysma work and botulinum toxin sit alongside creams as other ways people address the aging neck [8][9].
infobox: Retinoids, N-acetyl glucosamine, peptides, vitamin K2
Tretinoin; approved for acne in the US in 1971 [12]
Cosmeceutical; US law does not recognise the term [14]

paras: Photoaging, the cumulative effect of ultraviolet exposure, degrades collagen and elastin and is a main driver of wrinkles and pigment change; the neck and upper chest are exposed areas, and Wikipedia notes the upper chest is commonly affected in Canadian women [4].

Muscle also contributes. The platysma is a thin sheet of muscle across the front of the neck; reduced tone and thinning with age can produce wrinkly skin and more noticeable vertical bands, sometimes called turkey neck, and Wikipedia notes weightlifting and facelift surgery can make bands more visible [10]. Creams act on skin surface and dermal matrix; they are not described as acting on the muscle.

Neck-specific products are positioned around the observation that consumer interest in anti-ageing is moving from the face to other regions, including the delicate neck skin [2]. Active ingredients in the trials include nitric-oxide-supporting ingredients, N-acetyl glucosamine, retinol with peptides, and menaquinone-7 (vitamin K2) [6][7][1][11]. Retinoids more generally include retinol and retinal, tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid), adapalene and trifarotene, the last approved in the US in 2019 [3].

Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) is described by Wikipedia as the most extensively studied retinoid for photoaging. It was developed for acne by James Fulton and Albert Kligman at the University of Pennsylvania in the 1960s, approved by the FDA for acne in 1971, and sold as Retin-A, Avita and Renova; topical use is associated with irritation, redness and sun sensitivity, and pregnancy use is contraindicated [12].

Retinol and retinal are the over-the-counter forms. Wikipedia reports that the body converts retinol to retinal and then to retinoic acid, that cosmetic retinol shows clinical improvement that is not maintained after use stops, and that it is chemically unstable, so formulators use derivatives and antioxidants [13]. A 2006 review of retinoids for skin aging concluded that many retinoids give histological and clinical improvement, mostly in photoaged skin, with irritation limiting use of tretinoin and tazarotene and retinaldehyde and retinol being considerably less irritating [5].

In the EU and UK, retinol in cosmetics has been limited since November 2025 under Commission Regulation 2024/996, with a lower ceiling for body lotions than for other leave-on products, according to Wikipedia [13]. Neck products sold as cosmetics sit in the US category some call cosmeceuticals; the FDA states the law does not recognise that category, and products that affect the body's structure or function are drugs [14].

Neck-focused trials have tested products built around other ingredients: a nitric-oxide-supporting cream [6], N-acetyl glucosamine for firming and pigmentation [7], and menaquinone-7 (vitamin K2) in a 2026 split-neck trial [11]. The trials had participants apply the creams twice daily, and sun protection is described as the most effective primary prevention of photoaging [4].

A dual-centre open-label trial of a nitric-oxide-enhancing neck cream used twice daily for 12 weeks in 26 women reported improvements from baseline of 21% in wrinkles and lines, 27% in texture and 26% in skin tone at 12 weeks. A second group of 10 women with photodamage used the cream together with a double-conjugated retinoid/AHA product at night on neck and decolletage and showed 34% improvement in decolletage photodamage; the cream was well tolerated [6].

A 2023 open-label, blinded trial enrolled 20 adults who applied the retinol, tripeptide and glaucine cream to face and neck for three months; investigators reported clinical and histologic improvement in all 20, including type I and III collagen and glycosaminoglycan immunostains [1].

A study of 85 adult women aged 35 to 65 with Fitzpatrick skin types I to IV used a neck cream twice daily over three months, with a virtual trial at baseline and later visits. Improvement was statistically significant for hydration, texture, wrinkles and laxity, and 94% of subjects noted improvement in at least one category [2].

A 16-week study of a neck and decolletage cream with N-acetyl glucosamine in 42 women who completed it reported significant improvement in dermatologist-graded aging parameters at each time point; chromameter readings of chest pigmentation were also collected [7].

A 2026 randomized, double-blind split-face/neck, vehicle-controlled trial of a 0.05% menaquinone-7 cream enrolled women aged 35-60 (30 completers), alongside laboratory work on skin cells under oxidative stress [11]. The available studies are product-specific; independent head-to-head comparisons were not found.
A 2006 review of retinoids for skin aging, which was not neck-specific, reported clinical and histological improvement with many retinoids, mainly in photoaged skin.[5]

People pursuing a smoother neck also use procedural options. A 1998 Dermatologic Surgery paper described botulinum toxin for the aging neck [8], and plastic-surgery literature on neck rejuvenation covers platysma tightening, liposuction and facelift techniques [9][10]. Creams, injectables and surgery address different structures: skin quality, muscle bands and loose tissue.

A case report documented allergic contact dermatitis to ethylenediamine, a component of aminophylline, in a neck cream [15]. Wikipedia notes that regulators advise against oral retinoids in pregnancy, that the American Academy of Dermatology states retinoids should not be used during pregnancy, and that evidence of harm from topical use is lacking, with a 2026 Nordic cohort study finding no increase in major birth defects [3].

Because most neck creams are sold as cosmetics, product claims are not reviewed the way drug claims are; Wikipedia notes that critics say the cosmeceutical label can suggest pharmaceutical-level testing [14]. Retinoid-containing products have pregnancy cautions from regulators and dermatology bodies, as noted above [3].

lore.intro: Neck-cream claims come mostly from product makers and the small studies they support, with sources on forums and social media limited; the claims below are as manufacturers and study authors state them.

claims.claim: Neck skin needs its own formula because it is thinner and more delicate
A retinoid neck cream smooths lines and improves texture and tone
Retinol gives retinoid results with less irritation
Creams can fix neck bands and sagging
Retinoid creams are safe for everyone
